lessons.title: Energy, Defence, and Import-Dependent Sectors Under Geopolitical Stress

body.text: Energy, defence, and import-dependent are not single trades. Each one splits into sub-segments that can move in opposite directions on the very same headline, and the label alone tells you almost nothing about which way a specific stock actually moves.

children.text: Chapter 2's sector sensitivity table used one illustrative beta per sector to keep the stress-testing math tractable. This chapter earns back that simplification's cost by going deeper into three sector groups that sit closest to the four channels this course has built around: energy, defence, and the broader universe of import-dependent businesses. Each turns out to be more internally divided than the summary table let on, and understanding that division is often more useful than the headline sector label itself.
Energy: Not One Trade, But Three

Calling something an energy stock says almost nothing about how it responds to a crude oil shock. Upstream producers sell crude and gain directly. Refiners and marketers sit in the middle, and their economics split further into a refining side and a retail marketing side that can move in opposite directions in the same quarter. Gas utilities face a different input entirely. And renewable power generators are barely touched by any of it.

body.caption: Energy is at least four different trades wearing one label

cells: Upstream E&P (ONGC, Oil India)
Positive
Sells crude at market-linked realisation prices; a windfall tax has, at times, clawed back part of the upside during a sustained spike
OMCs / Refiners (IOC, BPCL, HPCL)
Mixed, often negative in the short run
Refining margins can widen even as marketing margins get squeezed, or turn negative, if retail pump prices are frozen for political reasons
City Gas Distributors (IGL, Mahanagar Gas)
Negative
Input gas cost is linked to international benchmarks; margin depends on how much cost is passed through to CNG/PNG consumers
Renewables & Power Utilities
Largely neutral to positive
No direct fuel-price exposure; often gains a longer-term policy tailwind as energy security becomes a stronger political priority

body.text: The clearest example of the political overlay on this table: Indian retail petrol and diesel prices stayed frozen for roughly four months from November 2021 into March 2022, spanning key state elections, even as Brent crude rose sharply toward the Russia-Ukraine war. OMCs absorbed the gap through marketing losses that showed up clearly in their next reported quarter. An OMC's real-world crude-price beta is not a fixed number pulled from a formula. It depends partly on the domestic political and election calendar, not only on the international oil price.

body.title: Upstream E&P vs OMCs: Same Sector, Opposite Story

columns.label: Upstream E&P (ONGC, Oil India)
points: Revenue rises directly with crude realisation prices
Can face a windfall tax clawing back part of the gain during a sustained spike
A comparatively clean, direct positive-beta play on rising crude

columns.label: OMCs / Refiners (IOC, BPCL, HPCL)
points: Refining margins can widen even as marketing margins get squeezed at the same time
A retail fuel price freeze around an election can turn a crude spike into a reported quarterly loss
A far messier, politically-mediated exposure than the sector label suggests

children.text: Defence: Indigenisation Changes the Payoff Structure

markDefs.definition: The ratio of new orders received in a period to revenue billed in that same period. A ratio above 1 means the order backlog is growing faster than it is being converted into revenue, a forward-looking measure of demand rather than a backward-looking one.

children.text: Defence stocks, PSUs such as HAL, BEL, and Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, and private players such as Solar Industries, Paras Defence, and Data Patterns, tend to rally within days of any border tension or major arms deal headline. That sentiment reaction is real, but it usually runs well ahead of anything actually happening to earnings, because India's defence procurement cycle, from tender to delivery, is measured in years, not quarters. The metric that matters more than a single quarter's reported revenue is the order book and its

, which tells you about revenue visibility years out, not the next print. Running alongside this is the Atmanirbhar Bharat indigenisation push, rising domestic-content requirements across successive defence procurement policy updates, a structural rerating tailwind that operates independently of any single conflict.

children.text: Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 used crude oil as the headline example of import dependency, but it is far from the only one. India imports a large share of its edible oil consumption, palm oil mainly from Indonesia and Malaysia, and historically a meaningful share of sunflower oil from Ukraine and Russia. When the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted Black Sea shipping in 2022, sunflower oil supply tightened sharply, pushing India to lean harder on palm and soybean oil and adding to consumer food inflation for a period, a geopolitical transmission channel that has nothing to do with crude at all. Fertiliser inputs tell a similarly distinct story: Russia and Belarus are major global exporters of potash, and a disruption there raises India's import cost, but who actually absorbs that cost depends heavily on how tightly a specific product is regulated, urea is heavily subsidised and price-controlled, so a shock there mostly hits the government's subsidy bill rather than a listed company's margin or a farmer's retail price.

body.caption: Import dependency runs well beyond crude oil

cells: Crude Oil
Middle East conflict, sanctions on a major producer
OMCs, aviation, chemicals, and the broader current account deficit and INR
Edible Oils (palm, sunflower, soybean)
Black Sea shipping disruption, export restrictions by a producing nation such as Indonesia
FMCG and food processing companies, consumer food inflation, and by extension the RBI's inflation calculus
Fertiliser Inputs (potash, phosphates)
Sanctions or supply disruption from a major exporter such as Russia or Belarus
Government fertiliser subsidy outgo directly; listed fertiliser company margins more indirectly, depending on the product's price controls
Electronics & Semiconductor Components
Export restrictions or a regional conflict affecting a major chip-producing economy
Auto, consumer electronics, and telecom equipment manufacturers reliant on imported components

children.text: A company that imports a crude-linked input but also exports a meaningful share of its finished output in dollars carries a natural hedge: a weaker INR raises its import cost but simultaneously raises its dollar export revenue in rupee terms, partially offsetting each other without buying a single derivative contract. Screening for this is straightforward on a tool like screener.in: compare a company's raw material cost as a percentage of sales against its export revenue as a percentage of sales. High on both sides suggests a natural, if imperfect, hedge already built into the business. High import dependence with little or no export revenue is a business carrying real, unhedged geopolitical exposure worth flagging explicitly.

body.title: Deep-Dive One Sector Using Screener.in
steps: Pick one sector from this lesson, energy, defence, or an import-dependent consumer or chemicals business, and shortlist three listed companies in it
On screener.in, check each company's raw material cost as a percentage of sales and its export revenue as a percentage of sales, to gauge natural hedge coverage
For a defence company, look up its current order book and, if disclosed, its book-to-bill ratio over the last one or two years
For an OMC, check recent quarterly results for any mention of marketing margin or under-recovery, a sign retail pricing was not fully cost-reflective
Note which of the four geopolitical channels from Chapter 1 this sector is most exposed to, and keep this deep-dive as a template for the next sector you analyse

body.title: Who Actually Absorbs the Shock?
body.scenario: A major fertiliser-exporting country announces an indefinite ban on potash and phosphate exports following an escalating regional conflict, cutting off a meaningful share of global supply.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, who actually absorbs the cost of this shock in India, the government, listed companies, or consumers, and why might that answer differ by specific fertiliser product?
body.modelAnswer: The answer splits by how tightly each product is regulated. Urea is heavily subsidised and price-controlled, so a potash or phosphate cost spike mostly shows up as higher government subsidy outgo, with the retail price to farmers largely unchanged in the near term. Non-urea products such as DAP and NPK have a different, more flexible subsidy structure, so the cost is more likely to be split between higher government subsidy payments, some pass-through to farmer prices, and some margin compression at listed fertiliser companies if they cannot fully pass costs through quickly. The broader lesson is that for a heavily regulated commodity, who bears a geopolitical shock is itself a policy design question, not something a simple stock-market beta can answer on its own.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why might an oil marketing company (OMC) report a loss on its fuel marketing business even during a period when Brent crude prices are extremely high?
options: Because OMCs are legally barred from selling fuel during a crude price spike
Because the government has, at times, kept retail petrol and diesel prices frozen for political reasons, forcing OMCs to sell below their actual cost
Because refining margins always fall whenever crude prices rise
Because OMCs are required to divert profits into a national oil reserve fund during a price spike
body.explanation: This is the political-economy point from this lesson: retail fuel pricing in India is not always a clean market pass-through, and a frozen retail price during a crude spike, as happened from November 2021 into March 2022, can turn a rising-crude environment into reported marketing losses for OMCs, independent of what is happening on the refining side of the business.

body.text: The company names, sensitivity directions, sub-segment splits, import-dependency figures, and defence trend chart in this lesson are illustrative and built for teaching purposes, not stock recommendations or verified current statistics. Always check current financials, order books, and government policy before drawing an investment conclusion. This is educational content, not investment advice.

points: Energy, defence, and import-dependent are not single trades; each splits into sub-segments with different, sometimes opposite, sensitivities to the same geopolitical headline

An OMC's real-world crude-price beta depends partly on the domestic political and election calendar, not only on the international oil price, since retail fuel pricing can be frozen for political reasons

Defence stocks often rally on sentiment within days of a tension headline, but the order book and book-to-bill ratio, not the next quarter's revenue, is what actually drives the stock over 2 to 3 years, given India's multi-year procurement cycle

Import dependency runs well beyond crude oil, into edible oils, fertiliser inputs, and electronics components, each transmitting through a different mechanism, from company margin pressure to government subsidy outgo to consumer inflation

Screening a company's raw material cost and export revenue as a percentage of sales on screener.in is a fast way to gauge natural hedge coverage, a habit the next two lessons build on when they turn to currency and debt market transmission, then safe-haven positioning
